content: LL-37, also referred to as CAP-18 (cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide, 18 kDa), is a gene that encodes the sole member of the human cathelicidin family. Cathelicidin-related antimicrobial peptides are a group of polypeptides that are localized in the lysosomes of macrophages, polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs), and keratinocytes. These peptides play a pivotal role in the innate immune defense mechanisms of mammals, particularly in combating invasive bacterial infections. Patients with rosacea exhibit elevated levels of cathelicidin. Cathelicidin is enzymatically cleaved into the antimicrobial peptide LL-37 by the serine proteases kallikrein 5 and kallikrein 7. Overproduction of LL-37 is hypothesized to contribute to the pathogenesis of all subtypes of rosacea. In dialysis patients, higher plasma levels of LL-37, which are upregulated by vitamin D, are associated with a significantly reduced risk of mortality from infections. Specifically, dialysis patients with elevated LL-37 levels are seven times more likely to survive a year of kidney dialysis without succumbing to a fatal infection. Vitamin D enhances the genetic expression of cathelicidin, which demonstrates broad-spectrum microbicidal activity against bacteria, fungi, and viruses. SAAP-148, a synthetic antimicrobial and antibiofilm peptide, is a modified derivative of LL-37. It exhibits superior antimicrobial properties compared to LL-37. Notably, SAAP-148 has been shown to be more effective in eradicating bacteria under physiological conditions.
